1.pericope_label: Son of man, take up a lamentation for Pharaoh king of Egypt, and say unto him, Thou art like a young lion of the nations, and thou art as a whale in the seas
debates: Whether the second beast is a crocodile or a hippopotamus
What the land wherein thou swimmest is
Which year the oracle belongs to
outliers: Clarke suggests the hippopotamus rather than the crocodile, since the reference seems to be to its way of feeding, walking into the water and fouling it with its feet
Ellicott recovers a contrast lost in the English, that Pharaoh was called a young lion but was really a crocodile fouling the rivers
Ellicott takes the land of thine outflow as most probably the land of the inundations of the Nile, now to be watered with blood
Gill notes a variant in which one ancient version reads the eleventh year for the twelfth
themes: Ministers told to weep for those who will not weep for themselves
A worm-reading offered for filling the valleys with thy height
Two lamentations composed at different times and set together
Slain left in the deserts of Libya

7.pericope_label: Then will I make their waters deep, and cause their rivers to run like oil, saith the Lord God
debates: Whether the quieting of the waters is a promise or part of the devastation
What the darkened lights of heaven stand for
What the beasts beside the great waters represent
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch name two scholars who take the sinking of the waters as a diminution of the Nile continuing the devastation, and reject it on the force of the introductory word, holding the verse a promise
Ellicott renders deep as quiet and allows that many see a glance forward at a blessing still future, though he thinks it need not look so far
Wesley reads the same verse the opposite way, as universal sadness making the brisk rivers grow slow and heavy
Clarke reads the darkened heaven as the empire, the stars as dependent states, the sun as the king and the moon as the queen
themes: A political hippopotamus fouling the waters
Formal mourning said to be performed always by women
The other five planets offered for the bright lights of heaven
Water left untroubled because too few remain to swim or row

17.pericope_label: Whom dost thou pass in beauty? go down, and be thou laid with the uncircumcised
debates: Which year the second dirge belongs to
Whether the practice of circumcision in Egypt is at issue
Why the prophet is told to do what he only foretells
outliers: Clarke reports several manuscripts and one ancient version reading the eleventh year against the twelfth of the text
Ellicott holds that all question about whether the Egyptians practised circumcision is out of place, the word being the ordinary phrase for the heathen

Ellicott takes the command to cast them down as a forcible way of stating that what is declared will certainly happen; Keil and Delitzsch add that the lamentation is the word of God and has power to accomplish it
Ellicott explains the pronoun oscillating between masculine and feminine by the thought moving between the king and the kingdom
themes: A mummy richly painted and no better than another carcass
A grave among common people instead of a pyramid
Burial with the famous called a poor allay to the reproach of death
Helpers who bore themselves as gods lying neglected

22.pericope_label: There is Elam and all her multitude round about her grave, all of them slain, fallen by the sword, which are gone down uncircumcised into the nether parts of the earth
debates: Whether Elam is Persia or an earlier power out of whose ruin Persia arose
Whether the twenty-seventh verse denies these nations the honours of the rest
Who the princes of the north are
outliers: Ellicott prefers to identify Elam with Persia and holds the prophet anticipates the future, his thought looking to the ultimate result without weighing comparative dates
Ellicott would read the twenty-seventh as a question, which the Hebrew fully admits, rather than as a statement of a more disgraceful end
Wesley takes the same verse the other way, the leaders surprised and tumbled into pits with the rabble rather than buried with the pomp of the others
Ellicott distinguishes the word for princes here from the one used of Edom, taking it to imply vassal princes of Syria and Damascus rather than the far north
themes: Warriors buried with their weapons laid beside them
A great captain and a beggar knowing no more than each other
Circumcision retained by Edom and availing nothing
Nations placed in the pit before they had fallen
